hints: Notice the wire diameter is 1.6 mm, so first find the cross-sectional area using radius $0.80 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$ in $A = \pi r^2$.
Connect the 430 N tensile force to stress with $\text{stress} = F/A$, then relate stress to strain through the Young modulus.
Convert 130 GPa to $130 \times 10^9 \text{ Pa}$, calculate $\text{strain} = \text{stress}/E$, and check that strain has no unit.
walkthrough: Find the cross-sectional area from the diameter. Radius $r = 1.6/2 \text{ mm} = 0.80 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$, so $A = \pi r^2 = \pi(0.80 \times 10^{-3})^2 \approx 2.01 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^2$.
Calculate the tensile stress. $\text{stress} = F/A = 430 / (2.01 \times 10^{-6}) \approx 2.14 \times 10^8 \text{ Pa}$.
Use the definition of Young modulus $E = \text{stress}/\text{strain}$ within the limit of proportionality. Rearrange to $\text{strain} = \text{stress}/E$.
Substitute values with units. $E = 130 \text{ GPa} = 130 \times 10^9 \text{ Pa}$, so $\text{strain} = (2.14 \times 10^8)/(130 \times 10^9) \approx 1.65 \times 10^{-3}$.
Strain is a ratio of lengths so it is dimensionless, and to two significant figures this is $1.6 \times 10^{-3}$. This is option C.

options.A: This results from using the 1.6 mm diameter as the radius, giving an area four times too large and a strain of about $4.1 \times 10^{-4}$.
options.B: This is too small and does not follow from $\text{stress} = F/A$ with $A = \pi(0.80 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m})^2$ and $E = 130 \times 10^9 \text{ Pa}$.
options.D: This results from omitting $\pi$ and using $A = r^2$, giving a stress about $\pi$ times too large and a strain of about $5.2 \times 10^{-3}$.
